10.1002_adfm.202600035: Metal anode batteries, particularly divalent systems including magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca), are promising candidates for next‐generation energy storage due to their high natural abundance and superior theoretical energy densities. However, the electrode/electrolyte interphase remains the paramount factor limiting the reversibility and reaction kinetics of Mg and Ca metal deposition/dissolution. Unlike the ionic‐conductive interphase demonstrated in monovalent metal (Li and Na) anode systems, conventional electrolytes often form ion‐insulating layers on the surface of Mg and Ca anodes, putting a significant barrier for reversible stripping and plating. This review provides a systematic analysis of recent advancements in understanding how the passivation layers impact Mg 2+ and Ca 2+ transport and reduction, and how these interphases evolve during electrochemical cycling. We also scrutinize the chemical composition and microstructures of the interphases in relation to electrolyte formulations. By establishing a correlation among electrolyte chemistry, interphase properties, and electrochemical performance for Mg and Ca metal anodes, this work provides a roadmap for the rational design of effective interphases for viable Mg and Ca metal batteries.
10.1002_adfm.79529: Lithium dendrite formation in solid‐state lithium metal batteries originates not only from mechanical failure but also from spatially heterogeneous interfacial electrostatic fields that induce localized Li + accumulation. However, existing electrolyte designs mainly regulate mechanical strength or chemical interfacial reactions, while dynamic regulation of interfacial electrostatic disorder remains unexplored. Here, we introduce an interfacial potential homogenization enabled by polarization‐mediated regulation. A molecularly entangled PEO/polyurethane/MOF‐177 electrolyte is constructed, where polar polymer networks and MOF polarization domains cooperatively redistribute local electric‐field fluctuations. This electrostatic regulation homogenizes Li + flux, lowers migration barriers, and suppresses preferential lithium nucleation. Consequently, CPEZ exhibits an ionic conductivity of 1.9 × 10 −3 S cm −1 and a Li + transference number of 0.71, both measured at 60°C. The Li/CPEZ/Li cell cycles stably for 9000 h at 0.1 mAh cm −2 . The Li/CPEZ/LFP retains 90 % capacity after 5000 at 1 C, while Li/CPEZ/LFP retains 85% capacity after 500 cycles at 100°C and cycles stably for 150 cycles at −15°C. This work establishes electrostatic regulation via polar interactions as a transferable design principle for durable, wide‐temperature solid‐state lithium metal batteries.
10.1021_acsmeasuresciau.6c00055: Epitope-imprinted polymers (EIPs) represent an advanced evolution of molecular imprinting technology for selective bacterial recognition. By using short, surface-exposed peptide fragments derived from bacterial proteins rather than whole cells or full-length proteins, EIPs enable the formation of structurally defined and chemically robust recognition cavities with improved accessibility, stability, and reproducibility. To the best of our knowledge, this review provides the first dedicated and focused overview of EIPs in bacterial detection. The fundamental principles of epitope imprinting are discussed, including rational epitope selection, computational modeling, monomer optimization, imprinting strategies (bulk, surface, nanoMIP, and electropolymerization), and template removal approaches. Representative applications targeting clinically significant pathogens such as Mycobacterium leprae, Salmonella Typhi, and Neisseria meningitidis are critically examined, highlighting analytical performance parameters including detection limits, imprinting factors, selectivity in complex biological matrices, and integration with electrochemical and piezoelectric transducers. In addition to summarizing current achievements, this review evaluates practical limitations related to epitope accessibility, matrix interference, fabrication reproducibility, scalability, and hospital-based implementation. Emerging strategies, including AI-assisted epitope design, multiepitope imprinting, nanomaterial-enhanced architectures, and portable point-of-care systems, are discussed as potential solutions to improve robustness and translational applicability. By consolidating current progress and identifying key scientific and technological gaps, this work clarifies the position of EIPs as promising synthetic recognition elements for next-generation bacterial diagnostics in clinical, food safety, and environmental monitoring.
10.1021_acssuschemeng.5c12308: Alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) offers a cost-effective pathway for green hydrogen production. However, AWE performance is often limited by the membrane. Herein, we synthesized in situ ZrO2/CoOOH-x nanoparticles and employed them as both the catalyst and filler for an AWE composite membrane, which achieved highly efficient water electrolysis. Furthermore, the ZrO2/CoOOH-10 membrane demonstrated optimal hydrophilicity with a contact angle of 38.9°, a surface roughness of 149 nm, an area resistance of 0.2 Ω cm2, and a hydroxide conductivity of 278.4 mS cm–1. In an AWE electrolyzer with NiFe foam/NiMo foam electrodes as the anode and cathode, respectively, the ZrO2/CoOOH-10 membrane reached 1777 mA cm–2 at the cell voltage of 2.0 V in 30 wt % KOH (80 °C), while maintaining stable operation for 150 h. Mechanistic studies revealed that CoOOH had dual synergistic effects on AWE performance: (1) enhanced hydrophilicity and (2) improved ionic conductivity and electrocatalytic activity. This work establishes a new method for designing multifunctional membranes, significantly advancing the development of AWE.
10.1038_s41467-026-79001-x: Atomic surface manufacturing (ASM) of single-crystal 4H-silicon-carbide (4H-SiC) is fundamentally constrained by its extreme hardness and chemical inertness. Conventional Fenton-assisted ASM techniques require strongly acidic conditions, which fundamentally mismatches the optimal manufacturing environment for 4H-SiC and leads to low throughput and serious metal ion contamination. Here we report an orbital engineering strategy that creates asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites in a metal-organic framework (Cu/ZIF-8) to enable efficient Fenton-like catalysis under neutral pH conditions. The asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites significantly split copper d-orbitals, reconstruct the electronic structure, and reduce the ligand-to-metal charge transfer barriers, thereby accelerating the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox kinetics for the Fenton reaction. Meanwhile, the vast specific surface area of metal-organic framework exposes a wealth of Nx-Cu-Oy sites without the need for ions to leach, which not only reduces wafer contamination risk but also meets the green manufacturing requirements. Consequently, Cu/ZIF-8 delivers an enhanced •OH generation under a neutral environment and achieves an improved ASM throughput for 4H-SiC, setting a benchmark in ASM of 4H-SiC. This study offers an intriguing bridge between molecular orbital design and manufacturing engineering and offer useful insights for future catalyst design and application. By engineering asymmetric copper sites in a metal-organic framework, researchers enable neutral-pH Fenton catalysis for atomic-scale polishing of silicon carbide, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional acidic processes.
10.1039_d4ta05355a: The relationship of how the composition of the ternary rare-earth halide SSEs influences their crystal structure, ionic conducting and electrochemical properties has been fully investigated.
10.1109_tte.2026.3668831: Equalization systems significantly affect the performance and lifespan of battery packs. As battery packs increase in size and complexity, accurate and computationally efficient tools for evaluating equalizers become increasingly important. Mathematical modeling offers a practical alternative to real-time simulations and experimental testing, which can be costly and time-consuming. However, conventional modeling approaches often experience accuracy limitations during long-duration equalization, reducing the reliability of estimations. This paper presents simplified yet highly accurate mathematical models for various equalizers based on the conservation of energy. The models incorporate converter efficiency and use a closed-form interval-based approach that significantly reduces memory usage and computational load. A comprehensive comparison of equalizer performance is conducted using the proposed models, and novel metrics are introduced for improved evaluation of energy redistribution and loss. The results demonstrate that the proposed models predict equalization time and voltage with less than 1% error. In simulation and cycle-by-cycle-based approaches, the processing time increases to days as battery capacity grows; However, the closed-form model exhibits capacity-independent computation time, enabling high scalability for large EV packs. Furthermore, the results show that direct-cell-to-cell equalizers achieve higher energy transfer efficiency, while adjacent-cell-to- cell structures provide faster equalization, offering practical guidance for topology selection in EV applications.
